tools.title: Tactical vs strategic AI
tools.definition: Tactics: short-horizon, position-centred reasoning about where to be and what to exploit now; strategy: longer-horizon reasoning over the whole situation. The chapter treats both as support layers that feed movement, pathfinding and decision making.

hooks.clause: separate the operator's per-dispatch tactics from the roadmap's strategy

tools.title: Simple tactical movement

transform.reason: Choosing a destination needs candidate qualities and a distance-discount scoring rule.

tools.definition: Pick the nearby point whose quality for the wanted tactic is best after discounting for distance or travel cost, then move there.

tools.title: Naive Bayes pseudo-code

transform.reason: Count-based training and classification need model state and probability operations.

tools.definition: Training is counting attribute values per class; classification multiplies the relevant frequencies and the class prior and picks the maximum.

tools.title: Log-probabilities and zero counts

transform.reason: Numeric stabilization needs log-domain evaluation and a smoothing parameter in a classifier.

tools.definition: Implementation notes: sum logarithms instead of multiplying tiny probabilities, and smooth unseen attribute-class pairs so a single zero does not veto a class.

verified.note: T&F preview TOC p.xiv (7.5.2; detail model-knowledge)

tools.title: Decision tree learning

transform.reason: Tree induction needs labelled examples, split selection, and node construction.

tools.definition: Induce a decision tree (as used in chapter 5) automatically from examples, so the structure of the decision is learned rather than authored.

hooks.clause: derive the feedback rule tree from labelled corrections

tools.title: ID3

transform.reason: ID3 needs entropy calculations, recursive partitions, and stopping rules.

tools.definition: Recursively pick the attribute whose split most reduces uncertainty about the action, partition the examples on it, and stop when a partition agrees on one action.

tools.title: Entropy and information gain
tools.definition: Entropy measures how mixed the actions in a set of examples are; the gain of an attribute is how much splitting on it lowers that mixture.

tools.title: ID3 with continuous attributes

transform.reason: Numeric splitting needs sorted samples and threshold-search operations.

tools.definition: For numeric attributes, sort the examples and test candidate thresholds between adjacent values, choosing the binary split with the best gain.

tools.title: Incremental decision tree learning

transform.reason: Online tree learning needs persistent node statistics and structural update rules.

tools.definition: Update an existing tree as new examples arrive instead of rebuilding from all examples, needed for online use.

hooks.clause: update the compiled rules per new example instead of recompiling the corpus

tools.title: ID4

transform.reason: ID4 needs count updates, split comparison, and subtree replacement.

tools.definition: The incremental variant described: store example counts at each node, re-evaluate the best split when an example arrives, and rebuild a subtree whose chosen attribute no longer wins.

tools.title: Subtree thrashing

transform.reason: Thrashing control needs subtree-change history and a restructuring policy.

tools.definition: Incremental rebuilding can repeatedly discard and regrow subtrees when two attributes trade places, wasting the examples held below; later algorithms (ID5, ITI) restructure instead of discarding.

tools.title: Reinforcement learning

transform.reason: Reward learning needs states, legal actions, reward delivery, and value updates.

tools.definition: Learn what to do from rewards that arrive after the fact, by estimating the long-run value of each action in each state through repeated experience.

tools.title: Tactical locations as decision inputs

transform.reason: Decision queries need reachable-point predicates and a decision-model input contract.

tools.definition: Expose questions such as whether a reachable cover point exists to the decision tree or state machine, so tactics shape the choice of action, not only its execution.

hooks.clause: let role decisions read the record's tactical facts rather than re-deriving them

tools.title: The problem (states, actions, rewards)
tools.definition: The world is a set of states; in each the agent picks an action, moves to a new state and receives a reward that may be zero; the task is a policy that maximises reward over time.

tools.title: Q-learning (the algorithm)

transform.reason: Q-learning needs state-action values and a temporal-difference update operation.

tools.definition: Keep a quality value per state-action pair and nudge it toward the reward just received plus a discounted share of the best quality available from the next state.

tools.title: Q-table
tools.definition: The table of quality values indexed by state and action; its size, states times actions, is the method's main limit.

tools.title: Exploration vs exploitation

transform.reason: Exploration needs a legal-action sampler and a policy-selection operation.

tools.definition: Always taking the best-known action never discovers better ones; a randomness parameter decides how often to try something else.

hooks.clause: reserve some worker effort for unproven approaches rather than only the known path

tools.title: Q-learning pseudo-code

transform.reason: Training episodes need action execution, reward feedback, and value-table updates.

tools.definition: Loop: observe state, choose an action (greedy or random), act, read reward and new state, update the quality entry, repeat; restart after a bounded walk.

tools.title: Problem interface (data structures and interfaces)

transform.reason: The learner interface needs state transitions, legal actions, and reward semantics.

tools.definition: The learner talks to the game through a small interface: enumerate actions for a state, perform one and return the reward and resulting state; the game, not the learner, encodes the world.

hooks.clause: workers act through a narrow interface that reports outcome and new state

tools.title: Implementation notes (RL)

transform.reason: Implementation choices need a state encoding and explicit unseen-entry initialization.

tools.definition: Practicalities such as representing states compactly, handling unseen entries and running the learner offline over many episodes.

tools.title: Performance (RL)
tools.definition: Memory grows with states times actions and the iterations needed grow faster still; realistic only for small, discrete problems or offline runs.

tools.title: Tailoring parameters

transform.reason: Learner tuning needs update-rate, discount, exploration, and episode execution contracts.

tools.definition: The knobs: learning rate (how far each update moves), discount (how much future reward counts), randomness (exploration) and walk length (when an episode restarts).

tools.title: Weaknesses and realistic applications

transform.reason: A bounded RL application needs a tractable state space and a designer-aligned reward.

tools.definition: State explosion, slow convergence and reward design make RL rare in shipped games; it suits offline tuning of bounded choices, with the reward chosen to express the designer's intent.

hooks.clause: a reward for apparent approval trains sycophancy; design the signal for the real goal

tools.title: Generating the tactical properties of a waypoint

transform.reason: Annotation requires property definitions and geometry-to-property evaluation rules.

tools.definition: How a point gets its qualities: hand annotation by designers, or automatic evaluation of the geometry around it.

tools.title: Other ideas in reinforcement learning
tools.definition: Pointers beyond basic Q-learning: temporal difference learning, on-policy vs off-policy updates, and approximating the quality table with a neural network.

tools.title: Temporal difference learning

transform.reason: Temporal-difference learning needs value state and a bootstrapped update rule.

tools.definition: A family in which value estimates are updated toward later estimates rather than final outcomes; Q-learning is one member.

tools.title: On-policy vs off-policy learning

transform.reason: Policy-dependent targets need next-action choices and distinct value-update rules.

tools.definition: Updating toward the action actually taken (as in SARSA) learns the behaviour you run, including its exploration; updating toward the best action (Q-learning) learns the optimal policy regardless.

tools.title: Neural network value approximation

transform.reason: Value approximation needs a state-action encoder, neural model, and training target.

tools.definition: Replace the explicit quality table with a network that maps state and action to a value, trading exactness for coverage of huge state spaces.

tools.title: Artificial neural network

transform.reason: Network learning needs a topology, activation functions, examples, and weight updates.

tools.definition: Layers of simple weighted units whose weights are adjusted from examples; a general function approximator used in games mostly for classification.

tools.title: Overview (neurons, weights, activation, layers)
tools.definition: Each unit sums weighted inputs and passes the sum through an activation function; units are arranged in input, hidden and output layers.

tools.title: The problem (supervised classification)

transform.reason: Supervised classification needs an input schema, target labels, and a train-test protocol.

tools.definition: Given input vectors with known desired outputs, find weights that reproduce the outputs and generalise to new inputs.

tools.title: Multi-layer perceptron with backpropagation (the algorithm)

transform.reason: Backpropagation needs network state, differentiable activations, and gradient updates.

tools.definition: Feed inputs forward, compare outputs with targets, and propagate the error backward layer by layer, adjusting each weight down the error gradient by a learning rate.

tools.title: Activation function (sigmoid, threshold)

transform.reason: Activation choice needs neuron evaluation and a compatible gradient contract.

tools.definition: The squashing function on a unit's sum; a smooth sigmoid makes gradients available for training where a hard threshold does not.

tools.title: ANN pseudo-code

transform.reason: Neural training needs forward, error, backward, and weight-update operations.

tools.definition: Training loop: forward pass, error at outputs, backward pass computing per-unit error terms, weight updates; prediction is the forward pass alone.

tools.title: Visibility and cover sampling (ray casting)

transform.reason: Cover sampling needs a ray-query operation, sample distribution, and occlusion geometry.

tools.definition: Estimate cover and vantage by casting many rays from the point to sampled positions and counting what is blocked or visible; coarse sampling trades accuracy for offline time.

tools.title: Network data structures and interfaces
tools.definition: Weights stored per layer as arrays or matrices, with per-unit activations and error terms kept for the backward pass.

tools.title: Implementation caveats

transform.reason: Network preparation needs normalization, topology selection, and convergence criteria.

tools.definition: Normalise inputs, choose hidden-layer size by trial, expect slow or failed convergence, and beware that a trained net is an opaque table nobody can inspect or patch.

hooks.clause: an opaque learned rule cannot be audited the way a written rule can

tools.title: Performance (ANN)
tools.definition: Prediction is cheap and fixed-cost once trained; training is the expensive, usually offline, part.

tools.title: Other approaches (RBF, Hebbian, weak supervision)
tools.definition: Alternatives mentioned: radial basis function networks, Hebbian learning, and learning with weaker feedback than exact targets.

tools.title: Radial basis function network

transform.reason: Radial basis learning needs centres, distance kernels, and output-weight updates.

tools.definition: Hidden units respond to distance from a centre point in input space, so the net learns local bumps rather than global planes.

tools.title: Hebbian learning

transform.reason: Correlation learning needs paired activations and a connection-strength update rule.

tools.definition: Unsupervised rule: strengthen a connection when both its units are active together, letting a net learn correlations without targets.

tools.title: Deep learning
tools.definition: Neural networks with many layers trained on very large datasets with modern hardware; responsible for the recent AI headlines and, in games, mostly an offline or research tool.

tools.title: What is deep learning?
tools.definition: Depth lets successive layers learn features of features; specialised architectures (convolutional, recurrent) and GPU training made it practical.

tools.title: Data as the constraint
tools.definition: Deep methods need volumes of labelled or self-generated data games rarely have; where it exists (telemetry, self-play) it is the enabling asset and the main cost.

hooks.clause: corpus policy decides what learning is even possible

tools.title: Deep reinforcement learning (self-play)

transform.reason: Self-play needs a game simulator, reward protocol, neural learner, and training loop.

tools.definition: Combining deep networks with reinforcement signals from self-play, the approach behind recent board- and video-game results; cited as context rather than a shipped-game technique.

tools.title: Lighting-derived concealment

transform.reason: Concealment needs a lighting query and a light-to-quality conversion rule.

tools.definition: Derive a shadow or hiding quality from the level's lighting data instead of from geometry alone.

tools.title: Procedural content generation (PCG)

transform.reason: Content generation needs a generator, seed semantics, and playable-output constraints.

tools.definition: Creating game content (worlds, levels, plants, dungeons, buildings) by algorithm, for variety, replayability and reduced authoring cost; new as a chapter in this edition.

tools.title: Offline vs runtime generation

transform.reason: Generation timing needs a runtime budget, validation rules, and a curation process.

tools.definition: Generating in the studio lets designers curate the output; generating at run time gives endless variety but must be fast and must never produce an unplayable result.

hooks.clause: generate kit surfaces at export time where they can be inspected, not at first run

tools.title: Pseudorandom numbers
tools.definition: Deterministic generators that produce random-looking sequences; the foundation of PCG because the same seed replays the same content.

tools.title: Numeric mixing and game seeds

transform.reason: Seed mixing needs context identifiers and a deterministic random-value function.

tools.definition: Derive every random decision from a single world seed by mixing it with context (coordinates, object ids), so any part of the world can be regenerated independently and identically.

hooks.clause: seed every fixture so a failure replays exactly
content-stable identifiers from seed plus context

tools.title: Hash-based (stateless) randomness

transform.reason: Stateless randomness needs an input encoding and hash-to-sample mapping.

tools.definition: Instead of advancing one shared generator, compute a random value directly from a hash of seed and position, which removes order dependence between subsystems.

tools.title: Shareable seed as world identity

transform.reason: Seed identity needs deterministic generation and a replayable content-version contract.

tools.definition: A seed is a tiny, shareable description of a whole generated world, which players can trade and developers can reproduce bugs from.

hooks.clause: a run's seed and inputs are the reproduction recipe recorded in evidence

tools.title: Halton sequence

transform.reason: Low-discrepancy points need a base sequence and coordinate-generation operation.

tools.definition: A low-discrepancy sequence built from reversing the digits of integers in a chosen base; successive points fill space evenly rather than clumping like true randomness.

hooks.clause: spread periodic checks evenly over a window rather than at random

tools.title: Low-discrepancy vs random sampling

transform.reason: Sampler comparison needs coverage criteria and explicit random and quasi-random generators.

tools.definition: Quasi-random points cover space uniformly and converge faster for sampling but show visible regularity; coprime bases are needed per dimension to avoid correlation.

tools.title: Phyllotaxic angles

transform.reason: Spiral placement needs indexed point generation and radial-growth rules.

tools.definition: Place successive points on a spiral rotated by the golden angle, the sunflower-seed pattern, to distribute items evenly over a disc.

tools.title: Poisson disk sampling

transform.reason: Minimum-distance sampling needs candidate generation, spatial tests, and point insertion.

tools.definition: Generate random points that are never closer than a minimum distance, giving natural-looking scatter (trees, stars, enemies) without clumps or voids.

tools.title: Offline precomputation vs runtime evaluation of qualities

transform.reason: Choosing update timing needs invalidation rules and a computation-cost model.

tools.definition: Baking qualities offline is cheap at run time but stale when the level changes; evaluating live tracks change but costs frames.

hooks.clause: projections baked at publish time versus recomputed on read

tools.title: Dart throwing vs grid-accelerated Poisson disk

transform.reason: Sampling acceleration needs a grid index and equivalent candidate-acceptance tests.

tools.definition: Rejecting candidates by brute-force distance checks is simple but slow; a background grid of cell size tied to the minimum distance makes the check constant-time.

tools.title: Lindenmayer system (L-system)

transform.reason: String growth needs production rules, rewriting steps, and geometry interpretation.

tools.definition: A string-rewriting grammar: start from an axiom, apply production rules in parallel for several generations, then interpret the symbols (often as turtle drawing) to grow plants and branching structures.

tools.title: Simple L-systems

transform.reason: Deterministic rewriting needs an alphabet, axiom, productions, and branch stack.

tools.definition: Deterministic rules, one per symbol, with push and pop symbols for branching; a few generations produce convincing trees and ferns.

tools.title: Turtle interpretation

transform.reason: Turtle drawing needs geometric commands, heading state, and a branch stack.

tools.definition: Reading the final string as drawing commands (forward, turn, branch) converts the grammar's output into geometry.

tools.title: Adding randomness to L-systems

transform.reason: Stochastic rewriting needs alternative productions and normalized choice probabilities.

tools.definition: Give a symbol several alternative rules chosen by probability so each plant differs while sharing a species-like style.

tools.title: Stage-specific rules

transform.reason: Age-dependent growth needs symbol ages and generation-conditioned productions.

tools.definition: Make rules depend on the generation or age of a symbol so growth changes character over time, for instance branching early and leafing late.

hooks.clause: planning passes may apply different rewriting rules at different maturity

tools.title: Landscape generation

transform.reason: Terrain construction needs geometry generators and height-field modification operations.

tools.definition: Producing terrain, usually as a height map, by stacking generators (noise, faults) and modifiers (erosion, filtering) until it looks and plays right.

tools.title: Modifiers and height-maps

transform.reason: Modifier composition needs height-map operations and a stage-execution contract.

tools.definition: Represent terrain as a grid of heights and build the generator as a pipeline of modifiers, each transforming the whole map, so stages can be reordered and tuned independently.

hooks.clause: the feedback compiler as a pipeline of whole-corpus modifiers

tools.title: Noise
tools.definition: Per-cell random values; raw white noise is too jagged to be terrain, so it is smoothed or interpolated at a coarser scale (value noise).

tools.title: Perlin noise

transform.reason: Gradient noise needs seeded gradients, interpolation, and coordinate evaluation.

tools.definition: Gradient noise: random gradients at lattice points, interpolated smoothly between them, giving continuous, natural-looking variation with no visible grid.

tools.title: Automatically generating the waypoints

transform.reason: Point generation needs a sampler and a rule for retaining useful candidates.

tools.definition: Produce candidate points without a designer: from observed play, from a regular grid, or from random sampling, then keep the useful ones.

tools.title: Octaves (fractal summation)

transform.reason: Fractal summation needs noise sources and frequency-amplitude composition operations.

tools.definition: Sum several layers of noise at doubling frequency and halving amplitude so large features carry fine detail; persistence and lacunarity set the ratios.

tools.title: Midpoint displacement (diamond-square)

transform.reason: Recursive terrain synthesis needs subdivision, averaging, and seeded displacement.

tools.definition: Recursively subdivide the map, setting each new point to the average of its neighbours plus a random offset that shrinks with depth; a classic fractal terrain method.

verified.note: model-knowledge (not in TOC; named in assignment list)

tools.title: Faults

transform.reason: Fault terrain needs line sampling and signed height-field edits.

tools.definition: Repeatedly choose a random line across the map and raise one side while lowering the other; many iterations produce ridged, plausible terrain.

tools.title: Thermal erosion

transform.reason: Slope relaxation needs material transfer and neighbour-height updates.

tools.definition: Where a cell's slope to a neighbour exceeds a talus angle, move material downhill until it does not; smooths cliffs into scree slopes.

hooks.clause: entropy reduction as repeated local levelling where the gradient is too steep

tools.title: Hydraulic erosion

transform.reason: Water erosion needs flow, sediment transport, deposition, and time-step state.

tools.definition: Simulate rain depositing water that picks up sediment, flows to lower cells, and drops sediment as it evaporates; carves valleys and river beds.

tools.title: Altitude filtering

transform.reason: Height filtering needs a transfer function and a terrain-height update operation.

tools.definition: Apply a transfer curve to heights, flattening lowlands into plains or sea, exaggerating peaks or terracing, to shape the map's gameplay profile.

tools.title: Dungeon and maze generation

transform.reason: Interior generation needs connectivity constraints and a layout-construction method.

tools.definition: Algorithms that produce connected interior layouts: perfect mazes, room-and-corridor dungeons, and constrained variants.

tools.title: Mazes by depth-first backtracking

transform.reason: Maze carving needs a visited set, randomized traversal, and wall-removal operations.

tools.definition: Random depth-first walk over grid cells carving passages, backing up when boxed in; yields a perfect maze with long winding corridors and few short dead ends.

tools.title: Perfect maze
tools.definition: A maze in which every pair of cells is joined by exactly one route, i.e. a spanning tree over the grid.

tools.title: Minimum spanning tree algorithms

transform.reason: Tree construction needs weighted edges, component state, and corridor creation.

tools.definition: Randomised Kruskal or Prim over grid edges also yields perfect mazes but with a different texture (many short branches); the same tools connect generated rooms with minimal corridors.

hooks.clause: link records with a minimal connecting structure, then add shortcuts deliberately

tools.title: Learning waypoints from player behaviour

transform.reason: Trace-to-waypoint learning needs event features and a clustering or promotion rule.

tools.definition: Record where human players pause, fight or hide and promote those spots to tactical points.

hooks.clause: mine where operators actually intervene to place guidance

tools.title: Recursive subdivision

transform.reason: Subdivision needs partition geometry, gap placement, and room-connection rules.

tools.definition: Split the space recursively into chambers with a wall and a gap each time, or into rooms by binary space partitioning, then connect siblings; gives rectilinear, architectural layouts.

hooks.clause: decompose a planning space recursively and connect siblings explicitly

tools.title: Generate and test

transform.reason: Generate-and-test needs a candidate generator, validators, and rejection or repair rules.

tools.definition: Produce a candidate by any method, test it against playability constraints (connected, right length, difficulty) and discard or repair failures; the general safety net of PCG.

hooks.clause: refutation is the test half of generate-and-test for plans

tools.title: Shape grammar

transform.reason: Shape rewriting needs geometric productions, constraints, and a derivation operation.

tools.definition: Rules that rewrite shapes into arrangements of shapes (a facade into floors, a floor into windows), used to generate buildings and cities with consistent style.

tools.title: Running the grammar

transform.reason: Grammar execution needs shape matching, rule application, and termination criteria.

tools.definition: Repeatedly pick a non-terminal shape and apply a matching rule, tracking each shape's position and size, until only terminal shapes remain.

tools.title: Terminal and non-terminal shapes
tools.definition: Non-terminals are placeholders still to be refined; terminals are the geometry that is emitted; the split controls where generation stops.

tools.title: Planning (goal-directed derivation)

transform.reason: Goal-directed generation needs derivation search, geometric constraints, and goal tests.

tools.definition: Choose which rules to apply by searching toward goals or constraints (a door on the street side, a stair reaching every floor) rather than at random, so the output meets design requirements.

hooks.clause: drive planning rewrites by goals and constraints, not by whichever rule matches first

tools.title: Board game AI

transform.reason: Board search needs legal moves, successor states, terminal tests, and scoring.

tools.definition: Turn-based, perfect-information games are attacked by searching the tree of possible moves with an evaluation of positions; the chapter covers the search family, memory, Monte Carlo methods and knowledge.

tools.title: Game theory (as used here)
tools.definition: The vocabulary for classifying games so the right search applies: players, turns (plies), zero-sum scoring, perfect vs hidden information, deterministic vs chance moves.

tools.title: Types of games

transform.reason: Game assumptions need a defined board state, turn protocol, and outcome contract.

tools.definition: The chapter's core methods assume two players, alternating turns, zero-sum outcomes, no hidden information and no dice; each relaxation (more players, chance, hidden state) needs extensions.

tools.title: Ply
tools.definition: One player's move; depth is counted in plies so that a full round of both players is two plies.

tools.title: The condensation algorithm

transform.reason: Condensation needs candidate scores, neighbourhood tests, and a deletion operation.

tools.definition: Start from a dense candidate set, score each point's qualities, and repeatedly drop points that a nearby better point makes redundant until a sparse, representative set remains.

hooks.clause: condense near-duplicate ledger ideas to a representative, keeping the best-scored

tools.title: The game tree
tools.definition: Nodes are positions, edges are legal moves, leaves are finished games with known results; its size is branching factor to the power of depth, which rules out exhaustive search.

hooks.clause: the option tree of a plan explodes the same way; search it, do not enumerate it

tools.title: Branching factor and depth
tools.definition: The two numbers that size the tree: average legal moves per position and the number of plies searched; small changes in either swing cost exponentially.

tools.title: The static evaluation function

transform.reason: Position evaluation needs a feature schema and a score-combination function.

tools.definition: A fast heuristic scoring of a position from one side's view, exact at finished games and approximate elsewhere; the search is only as good as this function.

hooks.clause: a verifier's score of a state is a static evaluation whose quality bounds the review

tools.title: Minimaxing

transform.reason: Minimax needs move generation, recursive value backup, and a depth cutoff.

tools.definition: Assume each side plays the move best for itself: your layers take the maximum of child scores, the opponent's take the minimum, down to a depth limit where the evaluation function stands in for the rest.

tools.title: The minimaxing algorithm (depth-limited recursion)

transform.reason: Depth-limited search needs successor enumeration and recursive score propagation.

tools.definition: Recursive descent that returns the best score and the move achieving it, stopping at terminal positions or at the depth cutoff.

tools.title: Negamaxing

transform.reason: Negamax needs perspective-aware scoring and sign-changing recursive search.

tools.definition: Collapse the max and min layers into one by negating the score returned from the opponent's perspective, which requires the evaluation to be symmetric (zero-sum).

tools.title: AB pruning (alpha-beta)

transform.reason: Alpha-beta needs bound propagation, move traversal, and branch-cutoff operations.

tools.definition: Carry a lower bound (alpha) and upper bound (beta) through the search and abandon any branch that cannot beat them; with good move ordering it searches roughly the square root of the plain tree.

hooks.clause: a refutation of a plan branch prunes everything below it without further evaluation

tools.title: Move ordering

transform.reason: Move ordering needs candidate moves and a reorderable search traversal.

tools.definition: Examining likely-best moves first makes pruning cut far more; sources of ordering include the previous iteration's best move and heuristics such as recently refuting moves.

tools.title: Killer and history heuristics

transform.reason: Killer and history ordering need cutoff records and move-priority updates.

tools.definition: Move-ordering heuristics: try the move that refuted a sibling position (killer) first, and prefer moves that have caused cutoffs often across the search (history).

hooks.clause: reuse the objection that sank a sibling option before inventing new ones

verified.note: model-knowledge (not in TOC; named in assignment list)

tools.title: The AB search window

transform.reason: Search windows need alpha-beta bounds and fail-high or fail-low handling.

tools.definition: The interval between alpha and beta at the root; a narrower starting window prunes more but, if the true value falls outside, the search fails and must be rerun with a wider window.

hooks.clause: a tight budget window prunes work but needs a re-run rule when the estimate fails

tools.title: Redundancy radius / threshold
tools.definition: The distance or similarity within which two candidate points count as duplicates during condensation; a tuning knob between coverage and sparsity.

tools.title: Aspiration search

transform.reason: Aspiration search needs a prior score, windowed searches, and widening rules.

tools.definition: Start the root window around the value expected from the previous iteration and widen only on a fail-high or fail-low.

tools.title: Fail-high and fail-low
tools.definition: Outcomes of a windowed search that prove the true value is above beta or below alpha without finding it; they trigger a re-search with adjusted bounds.

tools.title: Negascout

transform.reason: Negascout needs null-window probes and conditional full-window searches.

tools.definition: Search the first move with a full window, then test every later move with a zero-width window to prove it is no better; re-search only the rare move that passes the test.

tools.title: Principal variation search (PVS)

transform.reason: Principal-variation search needs an ordered line and verification re-searches.

tools.definition: The near-identical idea under another name: trust the principal line, verify the rest cheaply; its efficiency depends on good move ordering.

tools.title: Transposition table
tools.definition: A hash-indexed memory of positions already searched, so a position reached by different move orders (a transposition) is evaluated once and its result reused.

hooks.clause: memoise results by content hash so re-derived states cost a lookup

tools.title: Hashing game states

transform.reason: State hashing needs a canonical state encoding and collision checks.

tools.definition: Reduce a whole position to a fixed-size number cheaply enough to do every node, with collisions rare enough to tolerate.

tools.title: Zobrist keys

transform.reason: Incremental hashing needs piece-position keys and reversible XOR updates.

tools.definition: Assign a random bit string to every piece-on-square combination and XOR the strings of the pieces present; a move updates the hash incrementally by XORing out the old placement and in the new.

hooks.clause: incremental index keys that update by delta rather than recomputation

tools.title: What to store in the table
tools.definition: Per entry: the score, whether it is exact or only a bound (from a pruned search), the depth it was searched to, the best move found, and enough of the key to detect collisions.

hooks.clause: a receipt records the value, how certain it is, and how deep the check went

tools.title: Hash table implementation
tools.definition: A fixed array indexed by part of the hash with the rest kept for verification; size is a memory budget decision made up front.

tools.title: Replacement strategies

transform.reason: Replacement needs table collisions, entry ages, search depths, and an eviction operation.

tools.definition: When a slot is taken: always overwrite, keep the deeper (more expensive) entry, or run two tiers; deeper-first preserves costly results but can clog the table with stale ones.

hooks.clause: evict cheap-to-recompute cache entries before expensive ones

tools.title: Waypoint tactics

transform.reason: Waypoint annotation and lookup require a tactical-property schema and query operation.

tools.definition: Attach tactical meaning to a sparse set of marked positions so characters can reason about place by looking up a point rather than analysing geometry at run time.

tools.title: Tactical analysis

transform.reason: A tactical analysis needs a specified location-level function and input state.

tools.definition: A value computed for every location in a level that summarises some tactical fact (who controls it, how dangerous it is, how visible), used by strategic and tactical decisions.

tools.title: A complete transposition table

transform.reason: Search caching needs typed score bounds, depth validity, and lookup-store integration.

tools.definition: The assembled component: lookup before searching a node, use a stored exact value or tighten the window from a stored bound, store after searching.

tools.title: Transposition table issues

transform.reason: Cache correctness needs collision detection and path-sensitive result-validity rules.

tools.definition: Hazards: undetected collisions returning wrong moves, search instability when stored bounds steer later searches, path-dependent rules (repetition) that a position hash cannot see, and memory pressure.

tools.title: Using the opponent's thinking time (pondering)

transform.reason: Pondering needs opponent-turn execution and speculative state reconciliation.

tools.definition: Keep searching while the opponent decides, usually along the expected reply, so the table is warm when the real move arrives.

hooks.clause: use operator wait time to pre-compute the likely next step

tools.title: Memory-enhanced test (MT) algorithms

transform.reason: Memory-backed tests need null-window search and valid transposition reuse.

tools.definition: Replace one wide search with a series of zero-window tests that each only ask whether the value is above a bound, relying on the transposition table to make repeated tests cheap.

hooks.clause: a gate as a boolean test, repeated with a moving threshold, is cheaper than a full grading

tools.title: Implementing test

transform.reason: Bound testing needs a zero-window search operation and score-bound semantics.

tools.definition: A test is an alpha-beta search with a window of zero width at a chosen bound; it returns a value that proves the true score lies above or below that bound.

tools.title: The MTD algorithm

transform.reason: Repeated bound tests need interval state, a test search, and convergence rules.

tools.definition: Repeat tests, each narrowing the interval that must contain the true value, until the bounds meet; the starting bound distinguishes the variants.

tools.title: MTD(f)

transform.reason: MTD search needs a prior guess, repeated bound tests, and shared cache state.

tools.definition: Start the tests from a good guess (the previous iteration's value) so few tests are needed; usually the fastest member in practice.

tools.title: SSS* and DUAL* as MTD variants

transform.reason: Test variants need configurable initial bounds and the same zero-window driver.

tools.definition: Starting the test sequence from the maximum possible value reproduces SSS*, from the minimum reproduces DUAL*; both are special cases of MTD rather than separate algorithms.

tools.title: MTD pseudo-code

transform.reason: The search driver needs bound updates and a persistent transposition table.

tools.definition: Driver loop around the test routine maintaining lower and upper bounds, with the transposition table shared across tests.

tools.title: Monte Carlo tree search

transform.reason: Tree sampling needs selection, expansion, rollout simulation, and reward backup.

tools.definition: Grow a search tree selectively by repeating four steps: select a promising leaf, expand it, play a random game to the end, and propagate the result back up; needs no evaluation function and can stop at any time.

hooks.clause: sample plan continuations to the end rather than scoring every branch statically

tools.title: Representing the game level for analysis
tools.definition: The set of locations an analysis is computed over: a regular grid (typical for strategy games), the pathfinding graph's nodes, or arbitrary regions.

tools.title: Pure Monte Carlo tree search

transform.reason: Pure sampling needs legal-move rollouts and persistent node win statistics.

tools.definition: The knowledge-free version: uniformly random rollouts and win-rate statistics only, strong in games where evaluation functions are hard to write.

tools.title: Flat Monte Carlo vs tree search

transform.reason: Monte Carlo comparison needs equivalent rollouts and flat versus tree sample allocation.

tools.definition: Flat sampling plays random games from each root move and picks the best average; building a tree focuses later samples on promising lines and converges to minimax values.

tools.title: UCT and UCB1

transform.reason: Exploration bonuses need node visit counts and a child-selection operation.

tools.definition: Select children by a score that adds an exploration bonus, shrinking with visit count, to the observed win rate, so the tree balances exploiting good moves against trying under-sampled ones.

hooks.clause: allocate worker attempts across approaches by observed success plus an under-tried bonus

tools.title: Rollout (playout)

transform.reason: Rollouts need a simulated game, move policy, and terminal-result evaluation.

tools.definition: A fast simulated game from a leaf to a result using a cheap move policy; its quality and speed set the whole method's strength.

tools.title: Adding knowledge

transform.reason: Knowledge injection needs rollout policies, priors, and compatible score updates.

tools.definition: Improve pure MCTS with heuristics: biased rollout policies, prior values for promising moves, cutting rollouts short with an evaluation, or learned move predictors.

tools.title: Opening book
tools.definition: A stored table of good moves for early positions, compiled from expert play, consulted before searching so the opening is strong and fast.

place.section: 9.6 Opening Books and Other Set Plays

hooks.clause: canonical dispatch openings looked up before any planning

tools.title: Implementing an opening book

transform.reason: Book lookup needs position keys, weighted move choices, and a search fallback.

tools.definition: Key the book by position hash to candidate moves with weights, choose among them with some randomness for variety, and fall back to search when the position leaves the book.

place.section: 9.6 Opening Books and Other Set Plays

tools.title: Learning for opening books

transform.reason: Book learning needs game outcomes and move-weight updates.

tools.definition: Adjust the weights of book moves from the results of games actually played, so losing lines fade and winning ones are preferred.

place.section: 9.6 Opening Books and Other Set Plays

tools.title: Set play books

transform.reason: Set plays need situation matching and an executable response-book format.

tools.definition: The same book idea for any recognisable situation, not only openings: pre-authored responses for recurring positions or end-game patterns, with endgame databases as the extreme case.

place.section: 9.6 Opening Books and Other Set Plays

hooks.clause: standard responses for recurring order shapes, with search only off-book

tools.title: Iterative deepening

transform.reason: Iterative search needs repeated depth limits, interruption, and completed-result retention.

tools.definition: Search to depth one, then two, and so on until time runs out, returning the deepest completed result; each pass orders moves for the next, so the repeated work costs little.

hooks.clause: deepen analysis pass by pass under a time budget, always holding a complete shallow answer

tools.title: Simple influence map
tools.definition: Each unit projects an influence that fades with distance; summing per faction and comparing factions yields which side controls each location and where control is contested.

hooks.clause: a heat projection over records showing where activity and risk concentrate

tools.title: Variable depth approaches

transform.reason: Variable depth needs line-specific extension, reduction, and pruning criteria.

tools.definition: Search some lines deeper and others shallower: extend volatile or forcing sequences, reduce or prune unpromising ones, instead of one fixed depth for all.

tools.title: Horizon effect

transform.reason: Horizon control needs volatility detection and continued search beyond unstable cutoffs.

tools.definition: A fixed depth cutoff lets a search misjudge a position in the middle of an exchange, pushing an unavoidable loss just past the horizon and calling it fine.

hooks.clause: do not judge a change mid-exchange; wait for the dependent steps to settle

tools.title: Quiescence search

transform.reason: Quiet-position search needs forcing-move generation and a stability stopping test.

tools.definition: At the depth limit, keep searching only capture-like or forcing moves until the position is quiet, then evaluate; the standard remedy for the horizon effect.

hooks.clause: extend verification until the volatile part of a change is settled

tools.title: Search extensions and reductions

transform.reason: Depth allocation needs forcing-move criteria and per-branch depth updates.

tools.definition: Rules that add plies for singular or forcing moves and remove plies for moves judged unpromising, reallocating effort inside a fixed budget.

tools.title: Bitboards
tools.definition: Represent a board as machine words with one bit per square so move generation and evaluation become bit operations; a speed technique for chess-like games.

verified.note: model-knowledge (not in TOC; named in assignment list)

tools.title: Game knowledge
tools.definition: Everything the program knows beyond search: how to value positions, which openings work, which patterns matter; knowledge trades against search depth.

tools.title: Creating a static evaluation function

transform.reason: Feature scoring needs measurable board features, weights, and evaluation operations.

tools.definition: Combine measurable features of a position (material, mobility, structure, safety) with hand-tuned weights into a fast score, iterating with test games to fix misjudgements.

hooks.clause: make review criteria explicit weighted features, then tune them against outcomes

tools.title: Feature weights

transform.reason: Feature weights need a position evaluator; steering weights do not score board positions.

tools.definition: The coefficients that turn features into one number; getting them right is most of the work and the natural target for learning.

tools.title: Learning the static evaluation function

transform.reason: Evaluation learning needs game examples or rewards and score-weight updates.

tools.definition: Tune the feature weights automatically from expert games, from self-play results or by temporal-difference updates toward later evaluations, usually offline.

tools.title: Turn-based strategy games

transform.reason: Strategy turns need multi-unit actions, resource state, and a turn-transition model.

tools.definition: Games with many units and many choices per turn, where the tree is astronomically wider than in board games and search alone cannot work.

related.title: Real-time AI in a turn-based game

tools.title: Influence decay function
tools.definition: The rule by which a unit's influence falls off with distance (linear, inverse, exponential), chosen for feel and cost; unit strength scales the source value.

tools.title: Impossible tree size
tools.definition: With dozens of units each having dozens of options, a single turn has more combinations than any search can touch; the decision must be decomposed and abstracted instead.

hooks.clause: decompose a wide planning space into near-independent sub-decisions

tools.title: Decomposition into sub-decisions

transform.reason: Decision decomposition needs subproblem boundaries and a coordination protocol.

tools.definition: Treat units or regions as largely independent problems, decide each with its own cheap method, and coordinate through a strategic layer rather than a joint search.

tools.title: Real-time AI in a turn-based game

transform.reason: Turn-based reuse needs a turn clock and a concrete real-time controller to run.

tools.definition: Use the real-time toolkit (decision making, tactical analyses, pathfinding, steering-like movement) inside each turn, treating the turn as a long tick rather than as a tree to search.

tools.title: Execution management

transform.reason: Frame management needs job state, run budgets, and interruption semantics.

tools.definition: Fitting all the AI into a fixed slice of each frame: deciding what runs when, how to stop and resume work, and how to spend less on what matters less.

tools.title: Scheduling

transform.reason: Scheduling needs behaviour jobs and a frequency-phase execution operation.

tools.definition: Run each AI behaviour at its own frequency and phase within the frame budget rather than everything every frame.

tools.title: The scheduler

transform.reason: The scheduler needs registration state, a frame clock, and due-job dispatch.

tools.definition: A component holding registered behaviours with a frequency (run every n frames) and a phase (offset) each, executing those due on the current frame.

hooks.clause: the harness scheduler assigns frequency and phase to recurring checks

tools.title: Frequency and phase

transform.reason: Frequency and phase need a frame clock and per-behaviour dispatch controls.

tools.definition: Frequency sets how often a behaviour runs; phase staggers behaviours of the same frequency so they do not all land on the same frame.

tools.title: Spikes (load coincidence)

transform.reason: Spike control needs job costs and a schedule that can be measured and changed.

tools.definition: Frames where many behaviours fall due together blow the budget; frequencies with common factors make such coincidences periodic.

hooks.clause: periodic checks that coincide produce attention spikes for the operator

tools.title: Automatic phasing

transform.reason: Phasing needs a load forecast and phase-selection operations.

tools.definition: Choose a new behaviour's phase by scanning ahead and picking the offset with the least load, or pick frequencies that are relatively prime, so spikes are avoided without hand tuning.

hooks.clause: assign lane slots to minimise coincident load

tools.title: Interruptible processes

transform.reason: Interruptible work needs resumable state and pause-resume operations.

tools.definition: Behaviours that can stop part way and continue next time they run, through threads, cooperative yielding or explicit state saving, so long jobs fit in slices.

hooks.clause: a worker checkpoints its state so a stop is a pause, not a loss

tools.title: Control, frontier and security readings
tools.definition: Derived readings from an influence map: the sign of the faction difference gives control, near-zero difference marks the frontier, and total friendly dominance gives how secure a spot is.

tools.title: Time-sliced execution (yield when the budget is spent)

transform.reason: Time slicing needs budget checks, saved progress, and resumable execution.

tools.definition: Give a behaviour a time allowance; it checks the clock and returns when the allowance is gone, keeping enough state to resume.

tools.title: Load-balancing scheduler

transform.reason: Adaptive budget sharing needs measured job runtimes and slice-allocation updates.

tools.definition: Measure how long each behaviour actually takes and hand out the frame's budget in proportion, so the slice adapts to real cost instead of assumed cost.

hooks.clause: allocate token and time budgets from measured consumption, not from estimates

tools.title: Hierarchical scheduling

transform.reason: Nested schedulers need parent-child budget propagation and job dispatch.

tools.definition: A scheduler can itself be a scheduled behaviour, so a character's internal behaviours share the slice the parent scheduler gives that character.

hooks.clause: nested budgets, a gate's sub-checks sharing the gate's allowance

tools.title: Priority scheduling

transform.reason: Priority scheduling needs weighted slices and minimum-service guarantees.

tools.definition: Weight the budget by behaviour priority so important behaviours get larger or more frequent slices, while guarding low-priority ones against starvation.

tools.title: Starvation

transform.reason: Starvation prevention needs service accounting and enforceable minimum allocations.

tools.definition: Low-priority behaviours that never run because higher ones always consume the budget; a scheduler must reserve a minimum share.

hooks.clause: low-priority follow-ups that never get a turn

tools.title: Anytime algorithm

transform.reason: Anytime computation needs interruptible refinement and a valid partial-result contract.

tools.definition: An algorithm that can return a usable answer whenever it is interrupted and a better one the longer it runs; the natural fit for time-sliced AI.

hooks.clause: planning passes should always hold a complete shallow answer that deepens with budget

tools.title: Best-so-far result
tools.definition: The current answer an anytime algorithm keeps ready, with some indication of how refined it is, for whoever interrupts.

hooks.clause: a verification that stops early reports its best-so-far judgment and its depth

tools.title: Level of detail (LOD)

transform.reason: Effort scaling needs a simulation-fidelity controller; visible zoom alone does not change AI cost.

tools.definition: Spend effort in proportion to how much the player can notice: full fidelity near the player, cheaper approximations far away or out of sight.

hooks.clause: attention level of detail, full scrutiny where the operator is looking

tools.title: Graphics level of detail
tools.definition: The rendering precedent: simpler models at distance; the chapter borrows the idea and the vocabulary.

tools.title: AI LOD

transform.reason: AI detail selection needs importance inputs and concrete fidelity-dependent controllers.

tools.definition: Choose each character's AI effort from an importance measure (distance, visibility, player interest) rather than running every character at full fidelity.

tools.title: Unknown units and fog of war

transform.reason: Belief-based fields need faction knowledge and observation-update contracts.

tools.definition: Only units a faction knows about contribute to its influence map; the analysis models belief, not ground truth, so it can be wrong in useful, believable ways.

hooks.clause: projections should state what the record knows, not what is true

tools.title: Importance measure
tools.definition: The value that drives LOD choices, typically distance to the player, line of sight and whether the player is interacting; it must be cheap to compute for everyone.

hooks.clause: the console's notion of what is in focus

tools.title: Scheduling LOD

transform.reason: Scheduling detail needs per-unit update frequencies and a behaviour scheduler.

tools.definition: Lower the update frequency of unimportant characters in the scheduler while keeping their behaviour unchanged.

tools.title: Behavioral LOD

transform.reason: Behaviour replacement needs low-cost variants and state-reconciliation rules.

tools.definition: Swap in cheaper behaviours for unimportant characters (teleport along a path instead of steering, skip pathfinding) and swap back as importance rises.

hooks.clause: summary projections for far items, detail for the focused one

tools.title: Entry and exit processing

transform.reason: Detail transitions need state projection and plausibility checks on entry and exit.

tools.definition: When a character changes LOD, run code that makes the transition plausible, for instance placing it where it should have reached, so the player never catches the switch.

hooks.clause: catching up a record's state when it comes back into view

tools.title: Hysteresis (LOD flicker)

transform.reason: Detail hysteresis needs persistent level state and distinct transition thresholds.

tools.definition: Use different thresholds for stepping up and stepping down detail so a character near a boundary does not flip levels every frame.

hooks.clause: beacons and status need hysteresis so they do not flicker at a threshold

tools.title: Group LOD

transform.reason: Aggregate simulation needs state merging and splitting; visible zoom cannot conserve that state.

tools.definition: Represent a distant crowd or army as one entity with aggregate state and split it into individuals, sampled from that state, when the player approaches.

hooks.clause: aggregate records as a group until inspected, then expand

tools.title: LOD in summary (combining the levels)
tools.definition: The levels compose: scheduling, behavioural and group LOD together with anytime algorithms give the AI a smooth cost curve from nothing to full fidelity.

tools.title: World interfacing
tools.definition: How AI learns about the game world and talks to it: pulling information by polling, receiving it by events, sharing it through stations, and limiting it to what characters could plausibly sense.

tools.title: Polling

transform.reason: Polling needs timed queries and a world-state query interface.

tools.definition: The AI asks the world for what it needs each time it runs; simple and self-contained but repeats checks whose answer rarely changes.

hooks.clause: a console that re-reads status on a timer

tools.title: Events

transform.reason: World events need change detection, event emission, and listener subscriptions beyond delivery policy.

tools.definition: The world notifies interested AI when something changes; cheap when changes are rare but needs delivery machinery and can reach characters that no longer care.

hooks.clause: beacons as pushed notices of change

tools.title: Limited influence radius
tools.definition: Capping how far each unit's influence spreads bounds the update cost at the price of ignoring long-range effects.

tools.title: Determining which approach to use

transform.reason: Query-versus-event selection needs change rates, reader counts, and both execution protocols.

tools.definition: Poll when the information changes often and is checked rarely by few; use events when it changes rarely but many want to know promptly; mixed systems are normal.

hooks.clause: choose push or pull per signal by change rate and audience

tools.title: Event manager
tools.definition: A central dispatcher: sources post events, listeners register for the kinds they care about, and the manager queues and delivers, decoupling the two sides.

hooks.clause: the loopback between console and resident as a typed event bus

tools.title: Event manager implementation
tools.definition: Event objects with type and payload, registration lists per type, a queue drained each frame, with options for priorities and time stamps.

tools.title: Deferred delivery and queue draining
tools.definition: Events are usually queued and delivered at a fixed point in the frame rather than immediately, which keeps timing predictable and avoids re-entrancy.

tools.title: Event casting
tools.definition: Limit who receives an event: broadcast to all, narrowcast to a list, or cast by region or distance so only nearby listeners hear a local happening.

hooks.clause: scope notifications to the roles and views that can act on them

tools.title: Inter-agent communication

transform.reason: Sending sightings or requests needs message emission; delivery policy alone cannot send them.

tools.definition: Characters send events to each other through the same manager, sharing sightings or requests, which is how simple cooperation is often wired.

hooks.clause: workers exchange findings through a shared typed channel, not through the operator

tools.title: Polling station

transform.reason: Shared polling needs query registration, cached answers, and refresh execution.

tools.definition: A shared component that polls an expensive question once per update and serves the cached answer to every character that asks, instead of each character polling separately.

hooks.clause: an index that is refreshed once and read by all projections

tools.title: Polling station pseudo-code

transform.reason: Polling updates need a refresh clock, query evaluation, and cache writes.

tools.definition: Register questions with a refresh frequency; on each update recompute the due ones; readers get the latest stored value and its age.

tools.title: Polling station performance
tools.definition: Cost falls from readers times questions to one computation per question per refresh, at the price of answers being up to one refresh old.

tools.title: Polling station implementation notes

transform.reason: Cache freshness needs invalidation signals and age-aware lookup semantics.

tools.definition: Practicalities such as refresh scheduling, invalidation when the world changes abruptly and exposing the answer's staleness to readers.

hooks.clause: every projection should carry its own age

tools.title: Influence map uses

transform.reason: Field consumers need an objective selector, frontier query, or route-cost rule.

tools.definition: Typical consumers: choosing where to attack or defend, finding the frontier, rating locations as safe, and biasing pathfinding away from enemy control.

tools.title: Abstract polling

transform.reason: Derived polling needs query composition and dependency-aware refresh rules.

tools.definition: Stations can answer derived, higher-level questions (is the player in cover, which side holds the bridge) computed from raw data, and can be layered on other stations.

tools.title: Sense management

transform.reason: Plausible perception needs modality models, occlusion tests, and per-unit knowledge state.

tools.definition: Restrict what each character knows to what it could plausibly perceive, routing information from the world through modelled senses rather than giving everyone the truth.

hooks.clause: give an agent what it would observe, not the whole state; omniscient context breeds false confidence

tools.title: Faking it

transform.reason: Simplified perception needs a detection rule and a fairness criterion.

tools.definition: Most games cheat: characters know the player's position outright or use a distance and cone test; cheap and often good enough, but it reads as unfair when noticed.

tools.title: What do we know?

transform.reason: Knowledge provenance needs fact storage, observation sources, and update rules.

tools.definition: Decide explicitly which facts a character may hold and how they were acquired; knowledge is an asset with a source, not a global.

related.title: Unknown units and fog of war (6.2.2)

hooks.clause: records state their provenance; a projection shows what is known, not what is true

tools.title: Sensory modalities
tools.definition: Sight, hearing, touch and the rest, each with its own rules for range, direction, attenuation and what blocks it; a signal is tested per modality.

tools.title: Sensory modalities as filters

transform.reason: Sensory filters need ordered geometric and intensity tests per modality.

tools.definition: Treat each modality as a filter a signal must pass (range, cone, line of sight, threshold intensity) before the sensor is told; filters compose and are cheap to evaluate in order.

hooks.clause: feedback rules as ordered filters a signal must pass before it reaches a reader

tools.title: Signal, intensity and threshold

transform.reason: Threshold sensing needs signal attenuation and an intensity-comparison operation.

tools.definition: A sensed event has an intensity that attenuates with distance and obstacles; a sensor perceives it only above its threshold for that modality.

tools.title: Notification delay
tools.definition: Perception takes time: sound travels, attention lags; the manager schedules the notification for later rather than delivering it instantly.

hooks.clause: model operator reaction latency rather than assuming instant attention

tools.title: Region sense manager

transform.reason: Regional sensing needs candidate lookup and modality tests before delayed message routing.

tools.definition: Divide the world into regions; when a signal is emitted, consider only sensors in the same or connected regions, apply each modality's tests, and queue notifications with appropriate delays.

hooks.clause: lanes as regions that bound which signals reach which checks

tools.title: Potential sensors
tools.definition: The candidate list a signal must be tested against, narrowed first by cheap region membership so expensive per-modality tests run on few.

tools.title: Terrain analysis

transform.reason: Static terrain qualities need geometry queries and an explicit quality function.

tools.definition: Compute static per-location qualities of the level itself, such as how visible, how hard to cross or how well covered a spot is, independent of where units currently are.

tools.title: Finite element model sense manager

transform.reason: Graph sensing needs modality-specific attenuation and signal-propagation operations.

tools.definition: Model the world as a graph of nodes joined by edges with per-modality transmission factors; a signal spreads node to node, attenuating by each edge, so walls muffle sound differently from how they block sight.

hooks.clause: propagate change notices along the record graph with attenuation per link type

tools.title: Sense graph
tools.definition: The nodes and weighted edges the finite element manager spreads signals through; usually derived from level regions and portals.

tools.title: Tools and content creation
tools.definition: The AI a game ships is shaped by the tools that let designers create and tune its knowledge; the chapter surveys where that knowledge comes from and the toolchain that carries it.

tools.title: Toolchains limit AI
tools.definition: A technique with no authoring or debugging tool behind it will be used badly or not at all; tool investment, not algorithm choice, often bounds the AI.

hooks.clause: the operator's console bounds which project practices actually get used

tools.title: Where AI knowledge comes from
tools.definition: Three sources for the data AI needs: designers authoring it by hand, algorithms deriving it from level geometry, and mining it from recorded play.

hooks.clause: corpus knowledge comes from hand rules, static analysis and mined history, and each needs its own tooling

tools.title: Knowledge for pathfinding and waypoints
tools.definition: The graphs, regions and tactical annotations pathfinding and waypoint tactics need, and the ways of producing them.

tools.title: Manually creating region data

transform.reason: Manual region authoring needs editable geometry and property-painting operations.

tools.definition: Designers place nodes or paint regions in the level editor and mark their properties; precise and intentional but slow and fragile when the level changes.

tools.title: Automatic graph creation

transform.reason: Navigation extraction needs walkability tests and graph or mesh construction.

tools.definition: Derive the navigation graph from the level itself: grids over walkable floor, meshes from walkable polygons, or visibility points at convex corners, then let designers correct it.

hooks.clause: build indexes from the content rather than maintaining them by hand

tools.title: Designer correction pass

transform.reason: Correction preservation needs stable generated identities and patch-reapplication rules.

tools.definition: Generated data is treated as a draft a designer reviews and patches, with patches preserved across regeneration.

hooks.clause: generated rules stay drafts until a reviewer marks them, and reviewer edits survive regeneration

tools.title: Geometric analysis

transform.reason: Geometry analysis needs spatial queries and explicit tactical-property derivation.

tools.definition: Compute tactical and navigation properties from geometry by sampling and ray casting: walkable area, cover, visibility, chokepoints.

hooks.clause: static analysis of the corpus as the geometric pass

tools.title: Visibility map
tools.definition: A per-location score of how much of the surroundings can be seen from, or can see, that spot; high values suit vantage points, low values suit hiding.

tools.title: Data mining (from play)

transform.reason: Trace mining needs recorded events, clustering rules, and graph-generation operations.

tools.definition: Record where testers, players or exploring bots move, fight and pause, then cluster the traces into nodes, edges and tactical qualities.

hooks.clause: mine the control log for where operator effort and waits concentrate

tools.title: Exploration bots

transform.reason: Exploration needs a roaming controller and a trace-recording contract.

tools.definition: Automated agents that roam the level to generate movement data when human play data is scarce.

hooks.clause: automated probes that exercise the harness to generate coverage data

tools.title: Knowledge for movement
tools.definition: What steering and movement need from the content: what to avoid and where scripted motion should go.

tools.title: Obstacles (movement representation)
tools.definition: Steering needs a simplified view of obstacles (spheres, boxes, walls) separate from the full collision geometry; the tools must produce and keep it in sync.

tools.title: High-level staging

transform.reason: Staged motion needs authored marks, cue triggers, and a path-execution contract.

tools.definition: Designers lay out marks, paths and cues for where characters should move in set scenes, as a theatre director stages actors, and the AI fills in the motion.

tools.title: Knowledge for decision making
tools.definition: The vocabulary a decision maker reasons over: the kinds of things in the world and the actions it can actually take.

tools.title: Object types
tools.definition: A taxonomy of game objects with the properties the AI cares about, authored in tools so designers can add types without code changes.

hooks.clause: a shared schema of record kinds that roles reason over

tools.title: Concrete actions
tools.definition: Decisions must end in actions the game can execute (animations, state changes, effects), each defined and bound in the tools so the decision layer stays abstract.

hooks.clause: a role's decision resolves to a concrete, recorded operation

tools.title: The toolchain

transform.reason: Toolchain changes need artifact formats, stage interfaces, and rebuild rules.

tools.definition: The chain of software from authoring to running game through which AI knowledge flows; its shape decides who can change what and how fast.

tools.title: Integrated game engines
tools.definition: Off-the-shelf engines whose editors already carry navigation meshes, behaviour tree editors and scripting, lowering the cost of good AI at the price of fitting their model.

tools.title: Tactical location (rally point)
tools.definition: A position in the level annotated with the tactical qualities it offers, such as cover, concealment, a vantage point or an ambush spot.

tools.title: Terrain difficulty map
tools.definition: A per-location movement cost or accessibility value derived from slope, surface or obstacles, reusable as a pathfinding cost layer.

tools.title: Custom data-driven editors

transform.reason: Data editing needs a model schema, editor operations, and runtime reload semantics.

tools.definition: Studio-built editors that write data files the AI reads, so behaviour and knowledge change without recompiling and designers own the tuning.

hooks.clause: budgets and lanes as data files, not code constants

tools.title: AI design tools

transform.reason: Visual authoring needs editable decision nodes, validation, and runtime compilation.

tools.definition: Visual editors for state machines, behaviour trees and scripts that let non-programmers author decision logic and see it.

hooks.clause: the board as the authoring and reading surface for order logic

tools.title: Remote debugging

transform.reason: Live inspection needs state-access and mutation APIs plus synchronized visual overlays.

tools.definition: Connect a tool to the running game to watch and tweak AI state live, drawing paths, decisions and sensed knowledge over the world.

hooks.clause: loopback inspection of the resident's live state

tools.title: Plug-ins
tools.definition: Extend engines and editors through plug-in interfaces so AI middleware and studio tools slot into an existing pipeline.

hooks.clause: equipped support as plug-ins to the kit rather than forks of it

tools.title: Programming game AI
tools.definition: Practical choices about the language the AI is written in, when to move behaviour into scripts, and whether to build a language of your own.

tools.title: Implementation language

transform.reason: Language comparison needs a target workload and measured runtime or integration costs.

tools.definition: Each host language trades raw speed and memory control against productivity, safety and platform reach; the AI's needs (tight loops, many small objects, predictable frame cost) weigh the choice.

tools.title: C++
tools.definition: The traditional engine language: fastest and most controllable, with cache-aware data layout possible, but with manual memory management and complexity as costs.

tools.title: C#
tools.definition: The language of a leading engine's scripting layer: productive and safe, but garbage collection pauses punish allocation inside the frame.

tools.title: Swift
tools.definition: Apple's platform language: modern and safe with reference counting rather than a collector, relevant for mobile and desktop games on those platforms.

tools.title: Java
tools.definition: A managed, portable language with just-in-time compilation, central to Android; the same garbage-collection cautions apply.

tools.title: Learning with tactical analyses

transform.reason: Learning a map needs an event schema and an event-to-field update rule.

tools.definition: Treat a tactical map as something learned from play: accumulate events at locations and let old evidence decay so the map tracks how the level is actually used.

hooks.clause: a decaying map of where fixes and refusals cluster, learned from the control log

tools.title: JavaScript
tools.definition: The language of browser games: dynamic, single-threaded, fast under modern engines, but with unpredictable performance characteristics for heavy AI.

tools.title: Garbage collection pauses

transform.reason: Allocation control needs runtime memory operations, object lifetimes, and pause measurements.

tools.definition: Allocating in the per-frame path of a managed language triggers collections that stall frames; AI code pools and reuses objects instead.

tools.title: Lua and Python as host-side choices
tools.definition: The assignment list expected Lua and Python here; the public contents number only C++, C#, Swift, Java and JavaScript, and treat Lua and Python as embedded scripting candidates under 13.2.5.

tools.title: Scripted AI

transform.reason: Scripted control needs a script runtime, behaviour bindings, and reload semantics.

tools.definition: Behaviour written in a higher-level language or data form that the engine loads at run time, so designers can change it without recompiling the game.

tools.title: What is scripted AI?
tools.definition: Distinguishes scripting as an implementation vehicle for AI from scripted sequences as a design device; the former is the chapter's subject.

tools.title: What makes a good scripting language?

transform.reason: Language evaluation needs capability tests and workload-specific acceptance criteria.

tools.definition: Criteria: execution speed, compilation to a compact form, easy extension with engine functions, re-entrancy so scripts can pause and resume, and good debugging.

tools.title: Re-entrancy (coroutines)

transform.reason: Coroutines need saved execution state and yield-resume operations.

tools.definition: A script that can yield mid-way and continue next frame fits time-sliced execution; languages with coroutines make this natural.

hooks.clause: workers that can pause and resume at a recorded point

tools.title: Sandboxing and safety

transform.reason: Sandboxing needs a defined capability boundary and enforceable host-access rules.

tools.definition: Scripts should not be able to crash or corrupt the host; limits on what they can touch are part of the language choice.

related.title: What makes a good scripting language?

hooks.clause: refusals bound what equipped scripts may write

tools.title: Embedding

transform.reason: Embedding needs value marshalling, host bindings, and interpreter lifecycle operations.

tools.definition: Linking the interpreter into the engine, exposing engine functions and objects to scripts through bindings, and marshalling data across the boundary.

related.title: What makes a good scripting language?

tools.title: Choosing an open source language

transform.reason: Language selection needs explicit licensing, support, portability, and performance criteria.

tools.definition: Licence terms, maturity, community, portability to every target platform and performance all weigh in; an unmaintained or badly licensed language becomes a liability.

hooks.clause: the same tests apply to a kit dependency

tools.title: Frag map (danger map from recorded deaths)
tools.definition: The canonical learned analysis: each character death adds danger at its location, decayed over time, so characters avoid spots that have proven lethal.

hooks.clause: a heat map of where tests fail and gates refuse, with decay, to steer attention

tools.title: A language selection
tools.definition: Survey of embeddable candidates with their strengths and costs; Lua, Python, Lisp-family languages and others are compared.

tools.title: Lua
tools.definition: Small, fast, easy to embed, with coroutines and a permissive licence; the de facto game scripting language.

tools.title: Python
tools.definition: Rich libraries and readability, but larger, slower and harder to embed and to sandbox than Lua.

tools.title: Scheme and Lisp variants
tools.definition: Tiny, trivially parsed languages whose interpreters are easy to write and embed, at the cost of unfamiliar syntax for designers.

tools.title: Scripting vs other alternatives

transform.reason: Implementation choices need comparable behaviour models and change requirements.

tools.definition: Much of what scripting offers can come from data-driven behaviour definitions or visual tools; scripting earns its place when logic, not just parameters, must change without code.

tools.title: Creating a language
tools.definition: Building a scripting language from scratch, and the chapter's caution that it is rarely worth it compared with embedding an existing one.

hooks.clause: dispatch phrases are a tiny language; keep them a lookup, not a compiler

tools.title: Rolling your own

transform.reason: A language pipeline needs token, syntax, instruction, and host-binding interfaces.

tools.definition: The pipeline a home-made language needs: tokenizer, parser, compiler to an intermediate form, and interpreter, plus the tables that bind names to engine functions.

tools.title: Tokenizer

transform.reason: Tokenization needs lexical rules and token-stream generation.

tools.definition: Splits script text into tokens (names, numbers, symbols); the first stage of any language pipeline.

verified.note: model-knowledge (unnumbered in 3e TOC; named in assignment list)

tools.title: Parser

transform.reason: Parsing needs a grammar, syntax-tree construction, and positioned error reporting.

tools.definition: Builds a syntax tree from tokens according to the grammar, reporting errors with positions.

verified.note: model-knowledge (unnumbered in 3e TOC; named in assignment list)

tools.title: Compiler (to bytecode)

transform.reason: Compilation needs instruction semantics and syntax-to-bytecode translation.

tools.definition: Turns the syntax tree into a compact instruction stream that is cheaper to run than re-parsing text each time.

verified.note: model-knowledge (unnumbered in 3e TOC; named in assignment list)

tools.title: Decay rate as adaptivity knob
